title: Crop Rotation Basics
summary: Rotating between crop families (e.g. cereal -> legume -> oilseed) breaks pest and disease cycles that build up when the same crop is grown repeatedly, and legumes like gram or moong naturally replenish soil nitrogen for the next crop.
tips: Follow a nitrogen-hungry cereal (wheat, rice) with a nitrogen-fixing legume (chickpea, moong, soybean).
Avoid repeating crops from the same family (e.g. two Brassica crops back to back) in consecutive seasons.
Deep-rooted and shallow-rooted crops in rotation improve soil structure at different depths.

title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
summary: IPM combines cultural, biological, and chemical controls to manage pests with minimum chemical use, reducing cost and resistance build-up.
tips: Scout fields weekly and act only when pest counts cross an economic threshold, not on sight of a single pest.
Encourage natural predators (ladybird beetles, spiders) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticide overuse.
Use pheromone traps to monitor and mass-trap moths before resorting to spraying.
Rotate chemical classes if spraying is necessary, to slow resistance development.

title: Drip Irrigation Setup
summary: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, cutting water use by 30-50% compared to flood irrigation while often improving yield through consistent moisture.
tips: Filter water well before it enters drip lines - clogged emitters are the most common failure point.
Match emitter spacing to row spacing and crop root spread.
Combine with mulching to further reduce evaporation loss.
Government subsidy is often available under PMKSY - see Yojana Sathi for details.

title: Soil Health & Organic Matter
summary: Organic matter improves water retention, nutrient availability, and soil structure. Most Indian agricultural soils are low in organic carbon after decades of intensive cropping.
tips: Incorporate crop residue instead of burning it - stubble burning destroys organic matter and pollutes air.
Apply farmyard manure or compost between seasons to rebuild organic carbon.
Get a Soil Health Card (free, every 2 years) to track nutrient status over time - see Yojana Sathi.
Green manuring with dhaincha or sunhemp before a main crop adds nitrogen and organic matter cheaply.

title: Post-Harvest Storage Best Practices
summary: A large share of crop loss in India happens after harvest, from moisture, pests, and poor storage - not in the field.
tips: Dry grain to safe moisture content (usually below 12-14%) before storage to prevent fungal growth.
Store in clean, dry, pest-proof containers or bags, off the ground.
Use hermetic (airtight) storage bags for small quantities - they suffocate pests without chemicals.
Consider warehouse/cold storage financing under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund - see Yojana Sathi.

title: Understanding Fertilizer Ratios (NPK)
summary: Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), and Potassium (K) serve different roles: N drives leafy growth, P supports root and flower development, K improves overall plant vigor and disease resistance.
tips: Over-applying nitrogen without P and K can produce lush leaves but weak yield and lodging-prone stems.
Split nitrogen application (basal + top-dressing) rather than one large dose - reduces loss and improves uptake.
A Soil Health Card recommendation is more reliable than a blanket fertilizer ratio for your specific field.
Micronutrient deficiency (zinc, boron) is increasingly common in intensively cropped soil - watch for yellowing that doesn't match a typical N deficiency pattern.

title: Climate-Resilient Farming Practices
summary: With increasingly erratic rainfall and more frequent heat extremes, diversifying risk across practices matters more than optimizing for an average year.
tips: Choose short-duration or drought-tolerant crop varieties in areas with unreliable late-season rain.
Mulch to reduce soil temperature extremes and moisture loss during heat spells.
Diversify crops rather than relying on a single crop - reduces total-loss risk from any one weather event.
Check the Climate Risk & Yield page before major input investment decisions in a risky season.

title: Seed Selection & Treatment
summary: Seed quality and pre-sowing treatment strongly influence germination rate and early disease resistance.
tips: Use certified seed from a reliable source rather than saved seed of unknown disease status where possible.
Treat seed with a recommended fungicide or bio-agent (e.g. Trichoderma) before sowing to reduce seedling disease.
Do a germination test on a small sample before large-scale sowing to confirm viability.
Time sowing using the Weather Advisory page's sowing window guidance to avoid waterlogging or drought stress at germination.
